help-sidebar.motion.heading: Motion
help-sidebar.motion.item.turn-degrees.he:
Turn the `self` Sprite `angle` degrees anticlockwise (counter-clockwise).  To turn clockwise, use a negative number for `angle`.

```
# Turn a quarter-turn anticlockwise:
self.turn_degrees(90)
```

If you prefer, you can *augmented assign* to `self.direction`:

```
self.direction += 90
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.point-degrees.h:
Turn the `self` Sprite to point in the direction given by `angle`, which measures degrees anticlockwise (counter-clockwise) from its original orientation.  To give a direction in terms of rotation clockwise, use a negative value for `angle`.

```
# Point (1/8)th turn clockwise
# compared to original costume:
self.point_degrees(-45)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.direction`:

```
self.direction = -45
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.point-towards-m:
Turn the `self` Sprite to point in the direction of the mouse pointer.

```
# Point towards the mouse pointer:
self.point_towards_mouse()
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.go-to-xy.help:
Move the `self` Sprite to the position (`x`, `y`) on the Stage.

```
# Move to near top left:
self.go_to_xy(-200, 150)
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.go-to-mouse.hel:
Move the `self` Sprite to the position of the mouse pointer.

```
# Move to the mouse pointer:
self.go_to_mouse()
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.go-to-random-po:
Move the `self` Sprite to a random position on the stage.

```
# Go somewhere random:
self.go_to_random_position()
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.glide-to-xy.hel:
Glide the `self` Sprite smoothly to the position (`x`, `y`) on the stage.  The movement will take `seconds` seconds.

```
# Take 2½ seconds to move smoothly
# to the centre of the stage:
self.glide_to_xy(0, 0, 2.5)
```
Glide the `self` Sprite smoothly to the position of the mouse pointer.  The movement will take `seconds` seconds.

```
# Take 2½ seconds to move smoothly
# to the mouse pointer:
self.glide_to_mouse(2.5)
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.change-x.help:
Move the `self` Sprite horizontally by `dx`.  If `dx` is positive, move right; if `dx` is negative, move left.

```
# Move left a bit:
self.change_x(-20)
```

If you prefer, you can *augmented assign* to `self.x_position`:

```
self.x_position -= 20
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.set-x.help:
Move the `self` Sprite horizontally to the `x` position.

```
# Move horizonally to near the
# left edge of the stage:
self.set_x(-220)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.x_position`:

```
self.x_position = -220
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.change-y.help:
Move the `self` Sprite vertically by `dy`.  If `dy` is positive, move up; if `dy` is negative, move down.

```
# Move up a bit:
self.change_y(25)
```

If you prefer, you can *augmented assign* to `self.y_position`:

```
self.y_position += 25
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.set-y.help:
Move the `self` Sprite vertically to the `y` position.

```
# Move vertically to near bottom
# of stage:
self.set_y(-150)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.y_position`:

```
self.y_position = -150
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.x-position.help:
The horizontal position (`x` coordinate) of the `self` Sprite.

```
# Say how far left/right I am:
self.say(self.x_position)
```

You can assign to `self.x_position` to set the `x` coordinate of this sprite:

```
# Move sideways to three-quarters of the
# way from left to right:
self.x_position = 120
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.y-position.help:
The vertical position (`y` coordinate) of the `self` Sprite.

```
# Print how low/high I am to
# "Output" pane:
print(self.y_position)
```

You can assign to `self.y_position` to set the `y` coordinate of this sprite:

```
# Move up or down to three-quarters of
# the way from bottom to top:
self.y_position = 90
```
help-sidebar.motion.item.direction.help:
The direction the `self` Sprite is currently pointing, measured in degrees anticlockwise (counterclockwise) from its original orientation.

```
# Say what direction I'm pointing:
self.say(self.direction)
```

You can assign to `self.direction` to point this sprite in a particular direction:

```
# Point the opposite direction to default:
self.direction = 180
```
help-sidebar.looks.heading: Looks
Show a speech bubble for the `self` Sprite, saying `text`, lasting for `seconds` seconds.

```
# Ask nicely for an apple:
self.say_for_seconds("Apple!", 2)
self.say_for_seconds("Please?", 2)
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.say.help:
Show a speech bubble for the `self` Sprite, saying `text`.

```
# Greet everyone:
self.say("Hello world!")
```

If `text` is the empty string, remove the speech bubble for the `self` Sprite.  If the Sprite doesn't currently have a speech bubble, do nothing.

```
# Stop talking:
self.say("")
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.switch-costume.h:
Switch to one of the costumes listed in this Sprite's *Costumes* variable.  You can do this either by giving the costume's *name*, or its *number*.

```
# Switch to smiling costume:
self.switch_costume("smiling")
```

If you want to use a *number* to say which costume, remember that Python starts counting entries in a list at *zero*.

```
# Switch to first costume:
self.switch_costume(0)
```

```
# Switch to second costume:
self.switch_costume(1)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.costume_number` or `self.costume_name`:

```
self.costume_number = 3
# or
self.costume_name = "sparkly"
```

Switch to one of this Sprite's costumes.  You can do this either by giving the costume's *name*, or its *number*.

```
# Switch to smiling costume:
self.switch_costume("smiling.png")
```

If you want to use a *number* to say which costume, remember that Python starts counting entries in a list at *zero*.

```
# Switch to first costume:
self.switch_costume(0)
```

```
# Switch to second costume:
self.switch_costume(1)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.costume_number` or `self.costume_name`:

```
self.costume_number = 3
# or
self.costume_name = "sparkly.png"
```
Switch to one of the backdrops listed in your Stage's *Backdrops* variable.  You can do this either by giving the costume's *name*, or its *number*.

```
# Switch to sunny backdrop:
self.switch_backdrop("sunny")
```

If you want to use a *number* to say which backdrop, remember that Python starts counting entries in a list at *zero*.

```
# Switch to first backdrop:
self.switch_backdrop(0)
```

```
# Switch to second backdrop:
self.switch_backdrop(1)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.backdrop_number` or `self.backdrop_name`:

```
self.backdrop_number = 3
# or
self.backdrop_name = "sparkly"
```

Switch to one of the Stage's backdrops.  You can do this either by giving the costume's *name*, or its *number*.

```
# Switch to sunny backdrop:
self.switch_backdrop("sunny.jpg")
```

If you want to use a *number* to say which backdrop, remember that Python starts counting entries in a list at *zero*.

```
# Switch to first backdrop:
self.switch_backdrop(0)
```

```
# Switch to second backdrop:
self.switch_backdrop(1)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.backdrop_number` or `self.backdrop_name`:

```
self.backdrop_number = 3
# or
self.backdrop_name = "sparkly.png"
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.next-costume.hel:
Without `n_steps`, switch the `self` Sprite to the costume after the current one in the `Costumes` list.  If the Sprite was already wearing the last costume in the list, then switch back to the first one in the list.

```
# Switch to next costume:
self.next_costume()
```

You can also go forward more than one costume, or go *backwards* in the `Costumes` list, by giving `n_steps`.  With this usage, the `self` Sprite will switch to the costume `n_steps` after the current one.  If this would take the Sprite beyond the end of its `Costumes` list, then loop round to the start of the list, as if it was arranged in a circle.

```
# Switch to next-but-one costume:
self.next_costume(2)
```

Use a negative number for `n_steps` to switch to an *earlier* costume in the list.

```
# Switch to previous costume:
self.next_costume(-1)
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.next-backdrop.he:
Without `n_steps`, switch your Stage to the backdrop after the current one in the `Backdrops` list.  If the Stage was already showing the last backdrop in the list, then switch back to the first one in the list.

```
# Switch to next backdrop:
self.next_backdrop()
```

You can also go forward more than one backdrop, or go *backwards* in the `Backdrops` list, by giving `n_steps`.  With this usage, your Stage will switch to the backdrop `n_steps` after the current one.  If this would take the Stage beyond the end of its `Backdrops` list, then loop round to the start of the list, as if it was arranged in a circle.

```
# Switch to next-but-one backdrop:
self.next_backdrop(2)
```

Use a negative number for `n_steps` to switch to an *earlier* backdrop in the list.

```
# Switch to previous backdrop:
self.next_backdrop(-1)
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.set-size.help:
Set the `self` Sprite's size to `size`.  Scratch uses percentages for sizes, but in Pytch, `1` means the Sprite's normal size, `0.5` means half size, `2` means double size, and so on.

```
# Become three-quarter size:
self.set_size(0.75)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.size`:

```
self.size = 0.75
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.show.help:
Make the `self` Sprite visible.

```
# Appear:
self.show()
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.hide.help:
Make the `self` Sprite invisible.

```
# Disappear:
self.hide()
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.go-to-front-laye:
Move the `self` Sprite to the front drawing layer, making it appear 'closer' to the player than everything else.

```
# Move in front of everything:
self.go_to_front_layer()
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.go-to-back-layer:
Move the `self` Sprite to the back drawing layer, making it appear 'further' from the player than everything else.

```
# Move behind everything:
self.go_to_back_layer()
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.go-forward-layer:
Move the `self` Sprite `n_layers` layers forwards in the drawing order, appearing 'closer' to the player.

```
# Move three layers nearer front:
self.go_forward_layers(3)
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.go-backward-laye:
Move the `self` Sprite `n_layers` layers backwards in the drawing order, appearing 'further' from the player.

```
# Move four layers nearer back:
self.go_backward_layers(4)
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.costume-number.h:
The position in its `Costumes` list of the costume which the `self` Sprite is wearing.  Remember that Python counts list entries starting from *zero*. For example, if a Sprite is wearing its *third* costume, `self.costume_number` will be `2`.

```
# Say my costume number:
self.say(self.costume_number)
```

You can assign to `self.costume_number` to switch to a particular costume by (zero-based) *index*:

```
# Wear my fifth costume:
self.costume_number = 4
```
The position in its `Backdrops` list of the backdrop your Stage is showing.  Remember that Python counts list entries starting from *zero*. For example, if the Stage is showing its *third* backdrop, `self.backdrop_number` will be `2`.

```
# Print my backdrop number
# to the "Output" pane:
print(self.backdrop_number)
```

You can assign to `self.backdrop_number` to switch to a particular backdrop by (zero-based) *index*:

```
# Wear my fifth backdrop:
self.backdrop_number = 4
```
help-sidebar.looks.item.costume-name.hel:
The name of the costume which the `self` Sprite is wearing.

```
# Print my costume name to the
# "Output" pane:
print(self.costume_name)
```

You can assign to `self.costume_name` to switch to a particular costume by name:

```
# Wear my favourite costume:
self.costume_name = "sparkly"
```

The name of the costume which the `self` Sprite is wearing.

```
# Print my costume name to the
# "Output" pane:

```

You can assign to `self.costume_name` to switch to a particular costume by name:

```
# Wear my favourite costume:

```
help-sidebar.looks.item.backdrop-name.he:
The name of the backdrop which the Stage is showing.

```
# Print my backdrop name to the
# "Output" pane:
print(self.backdrop_name)
```

You can assign to `self.backdrop_name` to switch to a particular backdrop by name:

```
# Use my favourite backdrop:
self.backdrop_name = "sparkly"
```

The name of the backdrop which the Stage is showing.

```
# Print my backdrop name to the
# "Output" pane:
print(self.backdrop_name)
```

You can assign to `self.backdrop_name` to switch to a particular backdrop by name:

```
# Use my favourite backdrop:

```
help-sidebar.looks.item.size.help:
The current size of the `self` Sprite, where `1` is full size, `0.5` is half-size, `2` is double-size, and so on.

```
# Say how big I am:
self.say(self.size)
```

You can assign to `self.size` to set this sprite's size:

```
# Become twice normal size:
self.size = 2.0
```
help-sidebar.sound.heading: Sound
help-sidebar.sound.item.play-sound-until:
Start a sound playing and wait for it to finish.  The given `sound` can either be the name of the sound or its index (zero-based position) in the Sprite's (or Stage's) list of sounds.  This function will not return until the entire sound has played, so your code will not move on to its next statement until the sound is done playing.

```
# (This example is for a Sprite)
# Make noise, then disappear:
self.play_sound_until_done("splash")
self.hide()
```

Start a sound playing and wait for it to finish.  The given `sound` can either be the name of the sound or its index (zero-based position) in the Sprite's list of sounds.  This function will not return until the entire sound has played, so your Sprite will not move on to the next statement in the code until the sound is done playing.

```
# Make noise, then disappear:
self.play_sound_until_done("splash.mp3")
self.hide()
```

Start a sound playing and wait for it to finish.  The given `sound` can either be the name of the sound or its index (zero-based position) in the Stage's list of sounds.  This function will not return until the entire sound has played, so the Stage will not move on to the next statement in the code until the sound is done playing.

```
# Make noise, then change scenery:
self.play_sound_until_done("splash.mp3")
self.next_backdrop()
```
help-sidebar.sound.item.start-sound.help:
Start a sound playing.  The given `sound` can either be the name of the sound or its index (zero-based position) in the Sprite's (or Stage's) list of sounds.  Once the sound has started, the Sprite (or Stage) will straight away move on to the next statement in your code.

```
# (This example is for a Sprite.)
# Start playing tune, and glide
# to centre while tune is playing:
self.start_sound("my-song")
self.glide_to_xy(0, 0, 1.5)
```

Start a sound playing.  The given `sound` can either be the name of the sound or its index (zero-based position) in the Sprite's list of sounds.  Once the sound has started, the Sprite will straight away move on to the next statement in your code.

```
# Start playing tune, and glide
# to centre while tune is playing:
self.start_sound("my-song.mp3")
self.glide_to_xy(0, 0, 1.5)
```

Start a sound playing.  The given `sound` can either be the name of the sound or its index (zero-based position) in the Stage's list of sounds.  Once the sound has started, the Stage will straight away move on to the next statement in your code.

```
# Start playing tune, and count up
# the score while tune is playing:
self.start_sound("my-song.mp3")
for i in range(5):
    self.score += 1
    self.wait_seconds(1)
```
help-sidebar.sound.item.set-sound-volume:
Set the volume for sounds being played by the `self` Sprite (or Stage).  Volume values are measured between `0` (silence) and `1` (full volume), which is different from Scratch, which measures between `0%` and `100%`.

```
# Play fairly quietly:
self.set_sound_volume(0.25)
```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.sound_volume`:

```
self.sound_volume = 0.25
```

Set the volume for sounds being played by this Sprite.  Volume values are measured between `0` (silence) and `1` (full volume), which is different from Scratch, which measures between `0%` and `100%`.

```

```

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.sound_volume`:

```

```

Set the volume for sounds being played by the Stage.  Volume values are measured between `0` (silence) and `1` (full volume), which is different from Scratch, which measures between `0%` and `100%`.

If you prefer, you can assign to `self.sound_volume`:

help-sidebar.sound.item.change-sound-vol:
Increase the volume for sounds being played by the `self` Sprite (or Stage) by the given amount (or decrease the volume, if `d_volume` is negative).    Volume values are measured between `0` (silence) and `1` (full volume), which is different from Scratch, which measures between `0%` and `100%`.

```
# Play a bit more loudly:
self.change_sound_volume(0.1)
```

If you prefer, you can *augmented assign* to `self.sound_volume`:

```
self.sound_volume += 0.1
```

help-sidebar.events.heading: Events
help-sidebar.events.item.when-green-flag:
Ask Pytch to run the method below whenever the green flag is clicked by the player.

```
# Move to correct position
# when game starts:
@pytch.when_green_flag_clicked
def go_to_start_position(self):
    self.go_to_xy(20, 20)
```
Ask Pytch to run code whenever the green flag is clicked by the player.
help-sidebar.events.item.when-key-presse:
Ask Pytch to run the method below whenever the player presses the `key_name` key.

```
# Bark when player presses "b" key:
@pytch.when_key_pressed("b")
def bark(self):
    self.start_sound("woof")
```
Ask Pytch to run code whenever the player presses a particular key.
help-sidebar.events.item.when-this-sprit:
Ask Pytch to run the method below whenever the player clicks on this Sprite.

```
# Disappear if player clicks on me:
@pytch.when_this_sprite_clicked
def disappear(self):
    self.hide()
```
Ask Pytch to run code whenever the player clicks on this Sprite.
help-sidebar.events.item.when-stage-clic:
Ask Pytch to run the method below whenever the player clicks on the Stage.

```
# Make noise if player clicks on
# the Stage:
@pytch.when_stage_clicked
def beep(self):
    self.start_sound("beep")
```
Ask Pytch to run code whenever the player clicks on the Stage.
Ask Pytch to run the method below whenever any Sprite (or the Stage) broadcasts the `message`.

```
# Give player a point when they
# pop a bubble:
@pytch.when_I_receive("pop")
def give_player_point(self):
    self.score += 1
    self.say(self.score)
```
Ask Pytch to run code whenever any Sprite (or the Stage) broadcasts a particular message.
Broadcast the `message`.  This makes any methods with matching `@pytch.when_I_receive()` run.  Your method immediately continues running after the message has been sent.

```
# Tell cat it has been caught, and
# straight away start barking:
self.broadcast("caught-cat")
self.start_sound("woof")
```

(You might see `pytch.broadcast()`, which also works, in older code.)

Broadcast the `message`.  This runs any code under a matching *when I receive* hat block.  Your code immediately continues running after the message has been sent.

```
# Tell cat it has been caught, and straight
# away start barking:
self.broadcast("caught-cat")
self.start_sound("woof")
```

(You might see `pytch.broadcast()`, which also works, in older code.)

Broadcast the `message`.  This runs any code under a matching *when I receive* hat block.  Your code immediately continues running after the message has been sent.

```
# Tell cat it has been caught, and straight
# away show the sky backdrop:
self.broadcast("caught-cat")
self.switch_backdrop("sky.jpg")
```

(You might see `pytch.broadcast()`, which also works, in older code.)
help-sidebar.events.item.broadcast-and-w:
Broadcast the `message`.  This makes any methods with matching `@pytch.when_I_receive()` run.  Your method then waits until all methods which have responded to that message have finished running.

```
# Tell the dog to dance, and then
# praise it when it has finished:
self.broadcast_and_wait("dance")
self.say("Very good!")
```

(You might see `pytch.broadcast_and_wait()`, which also works, in older code.)

Broadcast the `message`.  This runs any code under a matching *when I receive* hat block.  Your code then waits until all code which has responded to that message has finished running.

```
# Tell the dog to dance, and then praise it
# when it has finished:
self.broadcast_and_wait("dance")
self.say("Very good!")
```

(You might see `pytch.broadcast_and_wait()`, which also works, in older code.)

Broadcast the `message`.  This runs any code under a matching *when I receive* hat block.  Your code then waits until all code which has responded to that message has finished running.

```
# Tell the dog to dance, and then show the
# sky backdrop when it has finished:
self.broadcast_and_wait("dance")
self.switch_backdrop("sky.jpg")
```

(You might see `pytch.broadcast_and_wait()`, which also works, in older code.)
help-sidebar.control.heading: Control
help-sidebar.control.item.wait-seconds.h:
Pause your code for `seconds` seconds.

```
# Wait for half a second:
self.wait_seconds(0.5)
```

(You might see `pytch.wait_seconds()`, which also works, in older code.)
help-sidebar.control.item.repeat.heading: Repeat
help-sidebar.control.item.repeat.help:
Run the indented code block the given number of times.  In Python, you can use the *loop variable* inside the block — it counts from zero up to one less than the number of times the loop runs, inclusive.

```
# Count from zero up to nine, writing the
# numbers to the "Output" pane:
for i in range(10):
    print(i)
```
help-sidebar.control.item.forever.help.f:
Run the indented block of code round and round forever.

```
# (This example is for a Sprite.)
# Make sure I am always saying the
# right score:
while True:
    self.say(score)
```
help-sidebar.control.item.forever.help.p:
Run the indented block of code round and round forever.

```
# Make sure I am always saying the
# right score:
while True:
    self.say(score)
```

help-sidebar.control.item.repeat-until.h:
To get the behaviour of Scratch's *repeat until* block, Python has the `while` statement.  This works the other way round to Scratch's *repeat until* block — Python runs the indented code while the test is *true*, compared to Scratch which runs the contained blocks while the test is *false* (i.e., until it's *true*).  Python's `not` operator can be useful, or you can sometimes rephrase the test instead.

```
# (This example is for a Sprite.)
# Move slowly up until I touch
# the Banana:
while not self.touching(Banana):
    self.change_y(2)
```

You can avoid `not` when using comparison operators — instead of `not n_clicks > 3`, you can say:

```
# Drift left until I have been
# clicked more than three times:
while n_clicks <= 3:
    self.change_x(-2)
```

```

help-sidebar.control.item.wait-until.hel:
To get the behaviour of Scratch's *wait until* block, you treat it like an empty *repeat until*, using Python's `while` statement.  This works the other way round to Scratch's *repeat until* block — Python runs the indented code while the test is *true*, compared to Scratch which runs the contained blocks while the test is *false* (i.e., until it's *true*).  Python's `not` operator can be useful, or you can sometimes rephrase the test instead.

To get *wait until* behaviour, you can use Python's `pass` statement inside the `while`.  The `pass` does nothing, but it is needed because Python needs *some* indented code for the `while` statement.

```
# Wait until player presses "d":
while not self.key_pressed("d"):
    pass
```

To replace *wait until score > 3*, you can avoid having to use `not` by saying:
```
# Wait until score > 3:
while score <= 3:
    pass
```

help-sidebar.operators.item.greater-than:
Report whether the first value is larger than the second value.  You often use this as part of an `if` or `while` statement.

```
# If player got a good score,
# congratulate them:
if score > 50:
    print("Well done!")
```

Python also has the `>=` operator, which means 'larger than or equal to':
```
# If player is at least 1.5m tall,
# tell them they can play:
if height >= 1.5:
    print("Let's play!")
```
help-sidebar.operators.item.less-than.he:
Report whether the first value is smaller than the second value.  You often use this as part of an `if` or `while` statement.

```

    print("Not many apples left!")
```

Python also has the `<=` operator, which means 'smaller than or equal to':
```

# high-score, encourage them:

    print("Try harder!")
```
help-sidebar.operators.item.equal.help:
Report whether the first value is equal to the second value.  You must use *two* equals signs for this in Python.  You often use this as part of an `if` or `while` statement.

```

if score == bot_score:
    print("It's a draw!")
```

help-sidebar.operators.item.logical-or.h:

help-sidebar.variables.heading: Working with variables
help-sidebar.variables.item.assign.help:
Make `variable` refer to `value`.

```
# Set the starting number of apples:
n_apples = 5
```
help-sidebar.variables.item.aug-assign-a:
Add `value_increase` to the value currently referred to by `variable`.

```
# The player got three more pears:
n_pears += 3
```

If you want to *decrease* a variable, you can use the `-=` operator.

```
# The player lost two bananas:
n_bananas -= 2
```

You can use `*=` and `/=` in a similar way.

In Python, the `+` operator can join strings or lists as well as add numbers, and the `+=` operator works the same.

```
# Build up greeting:
greeting = "Hello, "
greeting += player_name
```
help-sidebar.variables.item.show-variabl:
Display a variable-watcher for the variable called `variable_name` belonging to the `self` sprite (or stage).  Usually, `variable_name` will be a literal string, being the name of the variable you would like to show.  A particular variable is only ever shown once, even if `show_variable()` is called many times for that variable.

```
# Show my health:
self.show_variable("health")
```

To show a global variable, use this alternative form:

```
# Show the global "score" variable:
pytch.show_variable(None, "score")
```

(You might see this general `pytch.show_variable()` form elsewhere in older code.)

To show a global variable, use this alternative form:

help-sidebar.lists.heading: Working with lists
help-sidebar.lists.item.append.help:
Add the `thing` as a new entry at the end of the list `things`.

```
# Record another size:
sizes.append("large")
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.delete.help:
Delete the entry at position `index` from the list `things`.  Remember that Python starts counting at *zero*, so to delete the *second* element of a list, `index` should be `1`, and so on.

```
# Delete the third colour:
del colours[2]
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.delete-all.help:
Delete all entries of the list `things`.

```
# Forget all high scores:
del high_scores[:]
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.insert.help:
Insert a new entry `thing` into the list `things`, so that `thing` ends up at position `index`.  Remember that Python starts counting at *zero*, so to insert a new entry in the *second* place of the list, `index` should be `1`, and so on.

```
# Add "basketball" at very start of
# list of sports:
sports.insert(0, "basketball")
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.subscript-assign:
Replace the entry at position `index` in the list `things` with `new_thing`.  Remember that Python starts counting at *zero*, so to replace the *second* element of a list, `index` should be `1`, and so on.

```
# Replace third flower with a rose:
flowers[2] = "rose"
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.subscript.help:
Give the element at position `index` in the list `things`.  Remember that Python starts counting at *zero*, so to get the *second* element of a list, `index` should be `1`, and so on.

```
# Announce the second animal:
print(animals[1])
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.index.help:
Report the smallest index where `thing` can be found in the list `things`.  Remember that Python starts counting at *zero*, so if `thing` is the *second* element of the list, the value `1` will be reported.

```
# Tell the player which fruit is the apple:
print(fruits.index("apple"))
```

Scratch reports `0` if `thing` is not in the list, but Python *raises an exception*.
help-sidebar.lists.item.length.help:
Report the number of elements in the list `things`.  This will be zero if the list is empty.

```
# Say how many vegetables there are:
print(len(vegetables))
```
help-sidebar.lists.item.contains.help:
Report (as `True` or `False`) whether the list `things` contains `thing`.

```
# Beep if "dots" is one of the patterns:
if "dots" in patterns:
    self.start_sound("beep")
```

help-sidebar.lists.item.choice.help.flat:
To use this function, you must have the line `import random` at the top of your program, just after the `import pytch` line.

Give a random element from the list `things`.  For `things`, you can give a literal list, or use a variable which refers to a list.

Literal list, using []:

```
# Pick a random cat:
cat = random.choice(["Lulu", "Daisy", "Olive"])
```
Using a variable:

```
# Create list of cats:
all_cats = ["Lulu", "Daisy", "Olive"]
# Pick one at random:
cat = random.choice(all_cats)
```

help-sidebar.instances.heading: Sprites, clones, and the Stage
help-sidebar.instances.item.the-original:
Give the original instance of the Sprite class `cls`.

```
# Say which costume the original Dog
# is wearing:
the_dog = Dog.the_original()
print(the_dog.costume_name)
```

As a convenience, the following Sprite properties have special behaviour, different to how properties normally work in Python:

* `sound_volume`
* `x_position`
* `y_position`
* `direction`
* `size`
* `costume_number`
* `costume_name`
* `distance_to_mouse`
* `touching_mouse`

Code which reads these properties on a Sprite *class* gives the value of that property for that Sprite's *original instance*.

This can be useful where, for example, one sprite needs to know where another sprite is.  Instead of the fiddly

```
print(SpaceShip.the_original().x_position)
```

you can instead just write

```
print(SpaceShip.x_position)
```

If your code is reading a Sprite's *own* properties, you should use the simpler and standard

```
print(self.x_position)
```

You can *not* use this shortcut to *write* ("assign") to any of another Sprite's properties.  E.g., this code will not work:

```
# Will give error!
SpaceShip.x_position += 10
```
help-sidebar.instances.item.all-clones.h:
Give a list of all clones of the Sprite class `cls`.  If `cls` has no clones, the list will be empty.

```
# Say how many Cat clones there are:
print(len(Cat.all_clones()))
```
help-sidebar.instances.item.all-instance:
Give a list of all instances of the Sprite class `cls`.  The first element of the list will be the original `cls`, followed by any clones.  If `cls` has no clones, the list will contain just one element, i.e., the original `cls`.

```
# Say how many Apples there are
# altogether:
print(len(Apple.all_instances()))
```
help-sidebar.instances.item.the-only.hel:
Give the only instance of the Stage class `stage_cls`.

```
# Say which backdrop the stage
# is showing:
the_sky = Sky.the_only()
print(the_sky.costume_name)
```

As a convenience, the following Stage properties have special behaviour, different to how properties normally work in Python:

* `sound_volume`
* `backdrop_number`
* `backdrop_name`

Code which reads these properties on the Stage *class* gives the value of that property for the (unique) Stage instance.

This can be useful where, for example, a sprite needs to know what backdrop the stage is using.  Instead of the fiddly

```
print(MyStageClass.the_only().backdrop_name)
```

you can instead just write

```
print(MyStageClass.backdrop_name)
```

If your code is in your Stage, you should use the simpler and standard

```
print(self.backdrop_name)
```

You can *not* use this shortcut to *write* ("assign") to any of the Stage's properties.  E.g., this code will not work:

```
# Will give error!
MyStageClass.sound_volume = 0.8
```
